text:
I went with the rx 580 8gb myself. My 2 cents to help some of you decide.

I tend to keep GPUs longer than most (upgrading from a GTX680), so the 2gb extra VRAM will help in the long run. Also, Radeon drivers tend to become better with age, wringing more performance out; conversely nvidia tends to have better performance out of the box, and doesn't really improve much. Also, the dx12 and Vulcan support for the long term is better on the Radeon, so that's another point for longevity.

Ofc, the miner craze has made the rx580 all but extinct (I got lucky and found one on cyber Monday for a good price). The 1060 is way cheaper rn. Also has much higher clockspeed and overclocking headroom. The rx580 can get maybe 1450 or 1500 if you're lucky. The gtx can go farther from what I hear.

If you're the type that wants to play games rn and want it cheaper, Gtx1060. If you're more about long term, the rx580.

author: @drees84

text:
+Hardware Unboxed (GENUINE, INFORMED COMMENT AHEAD!! REALLY. :) 
I was thinking about your mentions of usage date in your review(s). Pointing to how many players actually play a game, like you do with Ashes, Far Cry, and COD. It hits AMD much harder than nVidia obviously, but that's not my primary concern. I wonder how useful it actually is. 
First, you make these videos for individual consumers, right? Not companies, developers, or similar, that might profit from macro level data like that. While it is true that the likelihood of a viewer playing COD and/or Ashes is much lower than it is for Far Cry, probability doesn't matter for the individual viewer that actually does plays COD and/or Ashes. Whether many others play that game doesn't really matter in judging the performance they get in that game; again, a game he/she, that particular individual viewer, does play despite being all kinds of lonely in a virtual space, astronaut, dad's exploding home, war, or whatever... (I don't play COD either:)
I reckon, mentioning a game's player base as part of a GPU performance review tailored to individual consumers of those cards (not the games) is at the very least not useful. 
We might even call it a logical fallacy. Which refers to confusing unrelated data (x people play this game) with a premiss that leads to the proposed conclusion (gpu 'A' is better than gpu 'B') like, gpu 'A' gets 'X' fps more than gpu 'B' in game 'Y'.)

Second, rhetoric. This touches on a rather more sensitive topic. So, let me be clear off the bat; I am NOT calling you biased. With that out of the way, let's continue. :) As your video makes abundantly clear, AMD suffers more from this low user base-problem than nVidia. At least in your bench suite. (Cudo's to nVidia for knowing the market and optimising the right games; although, I'm on the fence whether proprietary stuff like Game Works really should be called 'optimisation'. But let's leave that for another time...) The negative rhetorical, say, 'residue' of player base-information in a video like this puts AMD at a disadvantage to nVidia, in the eyes of your viewers, the consumer, on the basis of what seems to be rather useless information in the first place. 

Again, I'm not calling bias! I am convinced you mention this out of genuine interest -perhaps even frustration. But, it must be noted that rhetoric, however subliminal, matters and AMD is taking the brunt of the damage here. For no good reason, which is important to remember.
Perhaps it's a good idea to consider whether to include player base-data in future reviews. Let me know what you think. Cheers!

p.s. despite the lengthy 'critique', I like your videos. otherwise I wouldn't have taken time to write this out. keep them coming. :)

text:
The problem with Doom as a benchmark is that Nvidia deliberately choose to to maximise there GPU architecture on current gen gaming, a few years back. Both Maxwell and Pascal are very much gaming oriented, and really, really good at DX11 and older games when optimised for them, and only this. 

The reason is that Nvidia schedules its rendercalls via its driver, while AMD uses a hardware scheduler. The advantage for Nvidia is that is saves die space and makes there GPU's cheaper to make. It also saves power and that largely accounts for the difference between Nvidia and AMD. In a DX11 game all rendercalls are submitted to one CPU core for processing. In exchange for a higher CPU overhead on this core, the Nvidia driver can shift more work to other cores while AMD is completely limited to one core. Is that core maxed out, then the GPU is bottlenecked while the Nvidia counterpart can still squeeze a few frames out. 

This is also how Gameworks ruins games. A Gameworks title has way to much CPU load on the core where rendercalls are made to. The Nvidia driver can offload some of these instructions to other drivers, thus minimizing the effect. Combine that with excess PhysX which is also dumped on that one CPU core and you get a trainwreck of a game. And that is why no Gameworks title should ever be benchmarked. They are a terrible indication of actual performance. 

DX12/Vulkan are completely different, and a revolution in API design. They no longer are limited to one CPU core for rendercalls, but can use multiple cores. This eliminates a GPU bottleneck that was forming, and becoming quite apparent. You can see it when you test a GTX1080 at 1080p. A higher clocked CPU like the 7700K is usually faster. That is because this GPU is completely dependent one this one core and a lot of CPU's are holding this GPU back. This is why 1080p testing with the GTX1080, let alone the Ti or Titan Xp is kinda stupid. It does not demonstrate what a CPU is capable of in the future, it shows current performance for DX11 where the only thing that matters is raw clockspeed and IPC, not the future of DX12 where multiple cores matter. Further all AMD, GCN based GPU's (7xxx series and up) are capable of accessing multiple cores with DX12, Nvidia GPU's are not. That is why GCN GPU's are faster in DX12 titles. In effect they can finally be used to there full potential, and that shows. GCN in the end is not a pure gaming GPU, but a jack of all trades, that actually does everything pretty damn good. GCN however does not do gaming as good as Pascal in DX11. The DX11 era is however coming to an end and with DX12 around the corner, there is no reason to opt for Pascal any more if you know what you are buying. 

A game like Doom therefore has nothing to do with AMD favouritism, but with hardware limits of Nvidia GPU's. There will be no magic driver that will fix Nvidia there lacking DX12/Vulkan performance. Quite the opposite, AMD will only extent there lead with better drivers for games running on those API. Polaris 20 (RX580) in the end is also a better GPU than Pascal GP106 (GTX1060). It preforms better at higher resolutions, it competes with Nvidia in DX11 games which signals more raw power for Polaris 20 because Pascal is more efficient, and it handily defeats the GTX1060 in DX12 games, the future standard. 

Finally I kinda expect that Nvidia will go to a hardware scheduler with Volta. I doubt they have much choice in the matter, unless they like being ass kicked by AMD for the coming years in pretty much every major title. Vega in the end is a highly refined GCN GPU. AMD is taking a lot of there weaknesses and fixing them, making Vega potentially a very, very powerful GPU. It all depends on the drivers where they will end. Are the drivers good, then I would not be surprised to see the full Vega 10 GPU beating the GTX1080Ti.
